title-group.article-title: Post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome as a result of unilateral upper-lung field pulmonary fibrosis after lung cancer surgery: a case report

abstract.p: Post-pneumonectomy syndrome is a rare complication following pneumonectomy, characterized as significant mediastinal shift and rotation toward the operated side, resulting in stenosis of trachea and bronchi.

We report the case of a 60-year-old woman who underwent right lower lobectomy for lung adenocarcinoma in 2017. She subsequently developed unilateral upper-lung field pulmonary fibrosis (upper-PF) in the operated side, radiologically consistent with pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis, as a late surgical complication. By 2025, the resulting mediastinal right shift due to upper-PF caused the descending aorta to severely compress the left main bronchus, leading to acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. While typically recognized as post-pneumonectomy syndrome, this condition is extremely rare following lobectomy. This case demonstrates that unilateral upper-PF development can induce a post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome, even in patients who have not undergone a pneumonectomy.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Post-pneumonectomy syndrome is a rare complication following pneumonectomy, first described by Wasserman et al., in 1979 [1]. Significant mediastinal shift and rotation toward the operated side can lead to compression of the trachea and bronchi by the aorta or vertebral bodies, resulting in airway stenosis and marked exertional dyspnea [2]. While several cases have been reported after pneumonectomy, a similar mechanism occurring after lobectomy is extremely rare [3]. When this mechanism emerges without a history of pneumonectomy, it is referred to as post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome. It was first described by Veronesi et al., in 2002 in a patient who developed severe fibrosis and complete atelectasis of the left lung as a complication of chemoradiation treatment for recurrent mediastinal Hodgkin's lymphoma [4].

Recently, unilateral upper-lung field pulmonary fibrosis (upper-PF) radiologically consistent with pleuroparenchymal fibroelastosis (PPFE) has been reported to develop in the operated side as a late complication of lung cancer surgery [5]. Here, we report a case of post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome that developed following unilateral upper-PF development in the remaining lung after right lower lobectomy.

sec.title: Case presentation
sec.p:
A 60-year-old never-smoking woman underwent a complete thoracoscopic right lower lobectomy for Stage IA2 lung adenocarcinoma (pT1bN0M0) at a previous hospital in 2017 (Fig. 1A–B). Despite the absence of cancer recurrence, unilateral upper-PF lesion gradually emerged in the remaining right upper-lobe, which led to a significant mediastinal shift toward the operated side (Fig. 2A–B). In 2024, she was referred to our hospital due to pulmonary Mycobacterium kansasii infection in the left lower lobe and treated with antimicrobial therapy comprising isoniazid, ethambutol, and rifampicin (Fig. 2C). In August 2025, she was acutely admitted to another hospital with wheezing and dyspnea, was diagnosed with COVID-19. She rapidly developed acute hypercapnic respiratory failure requiring endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation, and was treated with remdesivir, systemic corticosteroids, and piperacillin/tazobactam. As she remained ventilator-dependent following acute management, a tracheostomy was performed, and she was transferred to our institution for continued care.Fig. 1
(A) Chest Xp and computed tomography (CT) images show apical cap in the right apex before surgery. Mixed ground-glass opacity was observed in the right lower lobe. (B) Seven months after lobectomy, right pleural effusion was present.Fig. 2
(A) The subpleural lesion with pneumothorax was observed two years after lobectomy. (B) The apical lesion apparently deteriorated five years after lobectomy. (C) Cystic change with pneumothorax and aggravated mediastinal shift was observed seven years after lobectomy in November 2024, when the patient was referred to our hospital due to pulmonary Mycobacterium kansasii infection. (D) Severe bronchial stenosis and mediastinal shift was observed when the patient was transferred to our institution, in September 2025. Esophageal dilation is observed.

Chest computed tomography (CT) demonstrated consolidation adjacent to the pleura and lung apex in the right lung, accompanied by bronchiectasis, cyst formation, and severe right lung volume loss (Fig. 2D). The mediastinum was markedly shifted to the right, leading to rightward rotation of the heart and a median position of the descending aorta. The left main bronchus was severely compressed by descending aorta and pulmonary artery. She remained on tracheostomy ventilation while pulmonary rehabilitation and nutritional support via a nasogastric tube were initiated. Ventilator weaning was unsuccessful because even brief daytime trials of spontaneous breathing were poorly tolerated due to severe dyspnea. Although her overall condition gradually improved, swallowing function remained impaired, characterized by significant laryngeal pooling of saliva and a weak swallow reflex. Fiberoptic endoscopic evaluation of swallowing yielded a Hyodo score of 8, indicating moderate dysphagia. The patient was ultimately transferred to a rehabilitation hospital with a convalescent ward offering swallowing rehabilitation by speech-language pathologists.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Unilateral upper-PF lesion radiologically consistent with PPFE has been reported to develop in the operated side as a late complication following thoracic surgery and show a course similar to idiopathic PPFE [[5], [6], [7]]. In patients who develop unilateral upper-PF after lung cancer surgery, several clinical features have been described, including the presence of an apical cap in the preoperative lung, postoperative pleural effusion at six months, and the emergence of aberrant intra/extra-thoracic air and cystic change during the clinical course [[5], [6], [7]]. In the present case, apical cap was observed in the right apex before surgery (Fig. 1A). Right pleural effusion was present seven months after lobectomy (Fig. 1B), and the subpleural lesion with pneumothorax emerged two years after lobectomy (Fig. 2A). Further, the apical lesion apparently deteriorated with cystic change (Fig. 2B–C). Therefore, this is a typical case of unilateral upper-PF after lung cancer surgery.

In the present case, left main bronchus was compressed by descending aorta and pulmonary artery and severely stenosed. This condition is generally known as post-pneumonectomy syndrome with an incidence of 2% of pneumonectomy. In patients treated with right pneumonectomy, the mediastinum shifts posteriorly and to the right, causing the heart and great vessels to rotate counter-clockwise and resulting in the compression of the left main bronchus between the left pulmonary artery and the spine or descending aorta [8]. On the other hand, in the case of lobectomy, the residual lung tissue typically prevents the mediastinal shift and rotation to some extent [9]. However, if the residual lung severely shrunk due to some factor and cannot prevent mediastinal shift, a post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome may develop. To date, there have been four reported cases which developed post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome (Table 1). All four patients underwent right lung lobectomy and possessed coexisting conditions that could cause a decrease in residual lung volume, such as radiation therapy, bronchial collapse, or atelectasis. In the present case, a remarkable volume loss of the remaining right lung occurred as a result of unilateral upper-PF development, which led to post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome.Table 1

In addition, the present case was complicated by nodular bronchiectatic Mycobacterium kansasii lung disease and COVID-19 pneumonia. These diseases are known to cause lung volume loss [12,13], and therefore may partially accelerate the progression of unilateral upper-PF, leading to the development of the post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome.

Furthermore, in the present case, moderate dysphagia was observed. To date, there have been a few cases of dysphagia which showed significant mediastinal shift compressing the esophagus after right pneumonectomy [8,14]. In the present case as well, CT imaging showed rightward tortuosity and dilation of the esophagus (Fig. 2D). These results suggest that anatomical alterations in post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome caused esophageal compression, leading to dysphagia.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: We report a rare case of unilateral upper-PF developing post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome. In the present case, unilateral upper-PF developed in the remaining lung after lobectomy and led to remarkable lung volume loss, resulting in significant mediastinal shift and rotation toward the operated side. Chest physicians and surgeons should recognize that unilateral upper-PF development potentially causes post-pneumonectomy-like syndrome, and thus careful long-term monitoring is essential.
